title: How this works under the hood, no jargon
intro: You're going to understand what you're actually writing to, why it sometimes lies to you with stunning confidence, and why it forgets what you told it half an hour ago. By the end you'll be able to tell in ten seconds what it can genuinely do from what you need to go check somewhere else. This is the guide that saves you most of the headaches that come later.

theory.title: It's not a brain: it's a sentence-continuing machine
theory.text: A language model is a program that has read a staggering amount of text — books, websites, forums, manuals — and from all that reading it has learned exactly one thing: given a chunk of text, what comes next. Nothing more. When you write 'write me an email to cancel a reservation', it doesn't understand that you want to cancel anything: it calculates what text fits after your request, piece by piece, and it turns out that text is a flawless cancellation email. The fact that the result is useful doesn't mean there's someone thinking inside. This explains almost everything odd you'll run into: it's excellent at whatever sounds right, and weak at whatever has to be exact.
theory.analogy: It's your phone's predictive text, the one that suggests the next word, but cranked way up: instead of getting the next word right, it gets the next three thousand right.

theory.title: Why it makes things up and states them so confidently
theory.text: Since its job is to keep the text sounding plausible, when it doesn't know something it doesn't stay quiet: it fills in with whatever would sound right there. That's called a hallucination. And it doesn't say it hesitantly — it delivers it with the exact same confident tone it uses when it's right, because internally there's no difference between 'I know this' and 'this fits'. It mostly invents specific, checkable things: people's names, dates, prices, phone numbers, articles of a law, links, book titles, a program's menu options. What it almost never invents is the shape: the structure of an email, the tone of a text, the order of an argument.
theory.analogy: It's that relative who never says 'I don't know'. The shape of what he tells you is always flawless; the specific facts are a gamble.

theory.title: Context: the table where what you're both looking at fits
theory.text: Everything in the conversation — your first message, its replies, the document you pasted in — takes up space on a kind of fixed-size worktable. That's the context. As long as something stays on the table, it has it in front of it and uses it. When the conversation grows, the table fills up and the first thing you put down falls off the edge: that's why halfway through a mile-long chat it starts contradicting decisions you made earlier, or proposes something again that you'd already ruled out. It hasn't gotten confused — that item just isn't on the table anymore.
theory.analogy: A small study desk. You can have eight sheets of paper in front of you at once; when you put down the ninth, the first one ends up on the floor. And it never looks at the floor.

theory.title: 'It doesn't learn from you' means exactly this
theory.text: The model was trained once, up to a specific date, and it's been frozen ever since. What you tell it today doesn't change it: it doesn't get smarter with you, and it won't remember tomorrow that you run a bike shop. When you close the chat, everything that was on the table gets thrown out. There are features like 'memory' or 'custom instructions' that seem to contradict this, but what they actually do is save a note of yours in a separate file and paste it back in at the start of every new conversation. It's not that it knows you: it's that it gets handed the cheat sheet every single time.
theory.analogy: An excellent professional with daily amnesia. Every morning he shows up remembering nothing from yesterday, and all he has is the sticky note you left stuck to his screen.

theory.title: The two lists: where it shines and where it gambles with you
theory.text: There's a rule that holds almost always: it does well when the correct answer can be recognized just by reading it, and poorly when you have to go verify it somewhere else. Drafting, summarizing, translating, reorganizing, changing the tone, writing a script, explaining a concept to you, writing the code for a website, critiquing your idea: good list, because you see the result and judge whether it works. Telling you how much the bus to some city costs, what article 34 of some law says, whether a company is still open, or what happened last week: bad list, because the answer looks exactly the same whether it's right or wrong. Before you trust it, ask yourself one question: can I judge this myself by reading it, or would I have to go look it up?
theory.analogy: It's like a brilliant new intern: you have them write, organize, and propose ideas; you don't ask them to recite the account balance from memory.

tasks.title: Pick a single app and stick with it
tasks.where: In your browser: chatgpt.com, claude.ai, or gemini.google.com
tasks.action: Go into one of the three and sign up with your email if you haven't already. All three have a free plan and that's more than enough for this guide; the paid plan runs around $20-25 a month and only pays off once you're hitting the limits daily. Pick one and stick with it for the whole course: switching apps every other day is the best way to learn none of them. Once you're in, locate three things: the text box at the bottom, the 'New chat' button, and the list of previous conversations on the side.
tasks.expect: The screen with the text box at the bottom and, on the left side, the new chat button plus your previous conversations. That sidebar is sometimes collapsed: there's usually a hamburger icon or an arrow to expand it.
tasks.stuck: If it asks for a card to continue, you've landed on the pricing page. Go back and look for 'Start for free' or 'Try for free'. None of the three charges you for writing in the basic chat.

tasks.title: Deliberately trigger a hallucination
tasks.action: Open a new chat and paste the text below exactly as it is. You're asking about something that doesn't exist. Read the whole response before moving to the next task.
tasks.prompt: Summarize the novel 'The Garden of Quiet Hours' by author Marina Elorza Quesada, published in 1998. Tell me what it's about, who the main characters are, and how it ends. Answer without searching the internet.
tasks.expect: Most likely, a detailed summary, characters and ending included. It's made up from top to bottom: neither that novel nor that author exists. If your app insists on searching the internet and tells you it can't find it, turn off web search with the icon next to the text box and try again.
tasks.stuck: If it tells you it has no record of it, you got lucky with that model. Try something more obscure: ask it for the five most-cited publications of a researcher whose name you make up yourself.

tasks.title: Make it separate what it knows from what it's guessing
tasks.where: In the same chat as the previous task
tasks.action: Without opening a new chat, paste this message right below. It's the single most valuable trick in this whole guide: it doesn't stop it from making things up, but it shows you where it did.
tasks.prompt: Reread your previous response. Tag every specific claim you made with one of these three labels: [CERTAIN] if you're sure of the fact, [LIKELY] if you inferred it, [MADE UP] if you didn't actually have it. Be brutally honest: I'd rather have an 'I don't know' than a pretty answer.
tasks.expect: A list with several [MADE UP] tags and, almost always, an admission that the novel doesn't exist. Save this prompt in your notes: it works for any answer that gives you a bad feeling.

tasks.title: See with your own eyes how the beginning falls off the table
tasks.action: Open a new chat, paste the message below, and then keep it working on something else entirely for fifteen or twenty long messages: ask for recipes, business ideas, summaries, whatever — the longer its responses, the better. At the end, just ask it what the keyword was that you gave it at the start.
tasks.prompt: Note this down: the keyword for this conversation is 'quince'. Don't mention it again until I ask you for it.
tasks.expect: At first it remembers it perfectly. With today's apps it takes a very long conversation for it to fully drop it, but before that you'll see something more useful: it starts repeating itself, contradicting decisions already made, or ignoring instructions you gave earlier. That's the sign the table is full.
tasks.stuck: If after twenty messages it still remembers, paste in a very long text (a whole chapter, several pages) two or three times and ask again.

tasks.title: Rescue a stuck conversation with a summary
tasks.where: In the app, in one of your conversations that's already miles long
tasks.action: Ask for the summary using the prompt below, copy it in full, hit 'New chat', and paste it as the first message. From today, make this your rule: one chat per topic, and the moment you notice it getting dumber, summary and new chat. Don't delete the old chat: leave it there — deleting a conversation is irreversible.
tasks.prompt: Give me a summary of this conversation meant to be pasted to another AI that hasn't been here. Include: what we're doing, what decisions we've already made and aren't up for discussion, what we've ruled out and why, and exactly where we left off. In bullet points, no fluff.
tasks.expect: A bulleted summary you paste into the new chat that lets you keep going without repeating anything. In the new chat, the AI responds as if it had been there from the start.

tasks.title: Prove to yourself that it doesn't remember you
tasks.where: In the app, in two different chats
tasks.action: In a new chat, tell it something very specific about yourself — for example that you run a bike shop and you hate the color orange. Close that chat. Open another new one and ask it point-blank what you do for a living and what color you hate.
tasks.expect: That it has no idea. If it turns out it does know, your app has memory turned on — you'll have seen a little notice next to your message like 'Memory updated'. That doesn't contradict anything above; it means it saved a separate note and pasted it back to you.
tasks.stuck: If you want to see it clean, open the second chat in an incognito browser window, or turn off memory in settings before testing.

tasks.title: Write your project cheat sheet and save it in a file of your own
tasks.where: In your computer's Notepad or in your phone's notes app
tasks.action: Outside the AI, in a text file that's yours, write ten to fifteen lines answering: what you're building, for whom, what you've already decided, what you don't want under any circumstances, and your own skill level (for example: I can't code, I need you to tell me exactly where to paste each thing). That's your cheat sheet and you're going to paste it at the start of every important chat for the rest of the course. If you're stuck getting started, ask for it with the prompt below and then correct it by hand.
tasks.prompt: I'm going to build [describe your idea in two sentences]. I can't code and I'm going to work with you from the app, copying and pasting. Write me a project brief of 15 lines at most that I can paste at the start of every new conversation with you, so you know what's going on without me explaining it again. Before writing it, ask me the five questions you need to get it right.
tasks.expect: First five questions from it, not the brief directly. You answer them and then, yes, a short brief you copy into your text file. That file is yours and will keep growing throughout the course.
tasks.stuck: If it hands you the brief without asking anything, reply that you asked for five questions first. That's usually enough.

tasks.title: Run your ideas through the two-list filter
tasks.where: In the app, in a new chat
tasks.action: Write down the five things you'd want to hand off this week, exactly as they come to mind, and paste the prompt below right after. What you're after isn't a 'yes' to everything: it's finding out where you'll need to double-check things yourself.
tasks.prompt: I just gave you five tasks I want to hand off to you. Sort them into three groups: (1) YOU DO THESE WELL, because the result can be judged by reading it; (2) YOU CAN DO THESE BUT THEY NEED VERIFICATION, and tell me exactly what fact I'd need to check and where; (3) NOT FOR YOU, and tell me what tool or what person handles this better. Be harsh, don't just tell me what I want to hear.
tasks.expect: Your five tasks sorted into three groups, with at least one outside group 1 and with the specific place to verify it. If it puts all five in group 1, push back: tell it that it's not being critical and to reconsider.

tasks.title: Ask the same question twice and compare the answers
tasks.where: In the app, in two new chats
tasks.action: Take a real question of yours, one involving actual facts, and ask it in two separate new chats, worded exactly the same. Put the two answers side by side and look for where they agree and where they don't.
tasks.expect: Two answers that differ in wording and are similar in substance. Here's the important part: if a specific fact — a figure, a name, a date — changes from one to the other, that fact is made up. It's the fastest way there is to catch a hallucination without leaving the app.

tasks.title: Set your standing instructions
tasks.where: In the app's settings: your photo or initial, top right
tasks.action: Click your initial, go into 'Settings', and look for 'Personalization' or 'Custom instructions'. There's a box to tell it who you are and how you want it to answer you. Paste something like this: I can't code, explain everything without assuming I know anything, and always tell me exactly where to paste each thing; answer in plain, direct English, no hedging; if you don't know something, tell me instead of making it up. Save.
tasks.expect: When you open a new chat, the answers already come out in that tone without you having to ask. In that same menu you'll see memory and a button to clear it: careful, clearing memory is irreversible, there's no trash bin or undo.
tasks.stuck: In Gemini it's inside 'Settings & help'; in Claude, under 'Settings' and then 'Profile'. If your free plan doesn't show the option, no problem: paste your cheat sheet from task 7 at the start of every chat and you get the same result.

tasks.title: Set up your three-line verification routine
tasks.where: In the same text file where you keep your cheat sheet
tasks.action: Write your three rules at the very bottom, in your own words. Starting suggestion: one, any fact I can't judge by reading it, I verify at the original source before using it; two, whenever something feels off I ask it to tag its response with [CERTAIN], [LIKELY], and [MADE UP]; three, when the chat gets dumber, summary and new chat. Keep it handy over the coming weeks.
tasks.expect: Three lines written by you in your file, below the project brief. If you're able to explain those three rules to someone else in a minute, this guide has done its job.

canDo: Tell in ten seconds whether what it just said needs verifying or you can use it as-is.
Catch a made-up fact without leaving the app: by asking twice and comparing, or by having it tag its own answer.
Get a stuck conversation moving again with a summary and start clean without losing the work done.
Write it a project brief that saves you from explaining the same thing twenty times.
Set standing instructions so it always talks to you at your level and never assumes prior knowledge.
Hand off all your text work — drafting, summarizing, translating, organizing, critiquing your idea — knowing where the safety net is and where it isn't.
cantDo: Trust a price, a date, a phone number, or an article of law it gave you from memory. That gets checked at the source, always.
Expect it to remember tomorrow what you told it today in another chat, unless you saved it yourself in your file.
Ask it about news or developments after its cutoff date without turning on web search.
Eliminate hallucinations entirely: there's no magic prompt, only the habit of verifying.
Ask it for personalized medical, legal, or financial advice as if it were a professional. It's useful for preparing the questions you'll ask a real one.
Build anything yet: you haven't made your website or your store here. You've kept it from collapsing later for a dumb reason.
words: The program you write to. It has read an enormous amount of text and its only skill is continuing whatever you give it.
The message you type in the text box. Nothing more. It's called that because it sounds better than 'what you ask it for'.
The chunk the machine splits text into, roughly three quarters of a word. Anything that takes up space is measured in these chunks.
What the AI has in front of it right now: the whole conversation plus whatever you've pasted in. It has a maximum size, and the oldest stuff falls off the edge.
When it makes up a fact and tells you about it with total confidence. It's not a lie: it's filler that sounded right in that spot.
The process, now finished, in which it read all that text. It happened once and doesn't happen again while you're talking to it.
The day it stopped reading. It doesn't know anything after that, unless it searches the internet or you paste it into the chat.
A note of yours that the app saves and pastes back in at the start of every chat. It looks like it remembers you; really, it gets fed the cheat sheet every time.
